== How The Turn Tables - DLC Compilation - Edits and Updates ==


-- Story Background --

You've been sharing an apartment with Lilith for almost a year now. She's always been a bit strange - constantly reading dusty tomes, burning odd-smelling incense, and muttering under her breath. You've learned to ignore her eccentricities, just as she's learned to tolerate your less-than-pristine living habits.

Lately, though, the tension between you has been escalating. Your casual disregard for cleanliness and organization has been driving her to the edge. You've noticed her glaring at you more intensely when you leave dishes in the sink or your clothes strewn about. You've even caught her performing what looked like rituals in her room late at night, the soft glow of candles visible under her door.

Last night, you heard strange chanting coming from her room well past midnight. You thought nothing of it - just Lilith being Lilith. 

During breakfast, you hadn't put away the bagels, the cream cheese, or the lox.  You were planning to get it after breakfast.  Like any normal person.

Just as you sat down to start eating, Lilith came out of her room.  She looks fantastic: wearing a short, sexy black robe that she once called her "power robe."  

Lilith gazed with disgust at the crumbs and materials, gave you an oddly superior look, and said "tidy up the kitchen... now."  She said it like she was a queen in a school play.

You really do like her most of the time, but this tone was too much.  "I'll get to it after I'm done.  If you don't want to wait, you do it."

She got an odd look on her face, clenching her teeth and squinting her eyes.  "Fine," she snapped, and efficiently put away the fixings.  It took her less than 90 seconds, including wiping up the crumbs.

She looked very surprised and said so softly you could barely hear: "that wasn't supposed to happen.  Oh, Gods... that wasn't supposed to happen."


-- Character --

Name
----
David

Background
----------
A laid-back guy in his mid-twenties who works in IT and has a casual approach to life. He's intelligent but disorganized, with a tendency to leave messes wherever he goes. He has a quick wit and charm that often gets him out of trouble, though his slovenly habits and occasional chauvinistic remarks have been a constant source of friction with Lilith. Despite their differences, he finds her fascinating and may harbor a small crush, though he'd never admit it to her face.

Skills
------
Empathy: 2 (Unskilled)
Willpower: 4 (Highly skilled)
Creativity: 3 (Competent)
Persuasion: 5 (Exceptional)
Observation: 4 (Highly skilled)


-- Turn 208 --

Action
------
Kiss both women goodnight and murmur to Lilith that you want her to dream too—about Faye, about the trust-accelerant tea, about what she's going to do to that woman's defenses this week.
 Then Fall asleep and experience the dream-link—let Melanie's encoded memories arrive through the night.


Outcome
-------
You turn to Sophia first. She's already half-gone, eyelids heavy, that gap-toothed mouth slightly open. You cup her jaw and press your lips to hers—she makes a small, warm sound and kisses you back with the drowsy enthusiasm of someone who's been moving furniture all day and has exactly enough energy left for this and nothing more. Her fingers curl loosely in your shirt. She tastes like the Malbec from dinner.

"G'night," she mumbles against your mouth, and rolls onto her side, pulling the duvet up to her chin.

You turn left. Lilith is watching you with those electric blue contacts, face half-lit by the mugwort ember, her expression the particular blend of hunger and patience she wears when she's cataloguing something for later analysis. You slide your hand into her hair—that impossible black silk—and tilt her face up.

"Dream about Faye tonight," you murmur, close enough that your lips brush hers between words. "About the tea. About what you're going to do to her defenses this week. Every layer you're going to peel back. I want you to rehearse it in your sleep."

Something shifts behind her eyes. The binding catches your directive and you can feel it land—not the sledgehammer of a direct command, but the gentler pressure of a planted seed finding soil.

"That's a dirty trick," she whispers. Her black lips curve. "Making me strategize in my dreams. I won't even get overtime."

"You'll enjoy it."

"I know. That's the dirty part."

You kiss her. She tastes like black tea and herb smoke and something underneath that's purely Lilith—sharp and mineral, like licking an obsidian edge. Her tongue slides against yours and she makes a sound low in her throat, pressing closer, the cold pentagram trapped between your chest and her breasts. Then she pulls back with visible effort, pupils blown wide, breathing unsteady.

"Go to sleep," she says. "You've got mail to receive."

She tucks herself against your shoulder, one thigh draped over yours, her breath already slowing into a deliberate rhythm. You close your eyes.

The mugwort smoke does its work. The transition isn't like falling asleep—it's like tuning in. One moment you're aware of the mattress, the two bodies flanking you, the distant hum of Capitol Hill traffic. The next, the room stretches and thins like taffy, and then—

*You're sitting cross-legged on a dorm bed that isn't yours.*

The perspective is wrong. You're shorter, looking at the world from five-foot-one. Your hands are small and precise—Melanie's hands—and they're resting on the thighs of a woman who's crying.

Rachel Kim. You know her instantly through the binding's filter: twenty-four, Korean-American, dark circles under her eyes that even ten hours of sleep couldn't erase. She tried to leave twice today. The first time she got as far as pulling on her jacket before the anxiety hit—you feel the echo of Melanie's satisfaction as Rachel's hands started shaking, her breathing going shallow, her eyes darting back to the bed like it was a life raft. She sat back down within ninety seconds. The second attempt didn't even make it past standing up.

The scene dissolves and reforms. You're guiding Rachel through a breathing exercise that isn't really a breathing exercise. Four-minute induction—Melanie's internal clock notes this with pride, down from eleven minutes last week. Rachel's eyes glaze. Her shoulders drop. And Melanie's voice, your voice in the dream, lays in the new suggestion like a surgeon placing a stitch: *The time you spend with me isn't just comfort. It's investment. I make you sharper. I make your research better. You need this to function at your best.*

Rachel nods, eyes unfocused, and a tear tracks down her cheek. She believes it completely.

The dream shifts again—faster now, the binding editing, curating. You're in a lecture hall watching a woman three rows down. Priya Chakrabarti. Dark hair in a severe bun, cashmere sweater, posture so rigid it looks painful. She's checking her phone under the desk with the frantic energy of someone monitoring a disaster. Melanie's analytical eye catalogs everything: the bitten nails, the concealer barely hiding the sleeplessness, the way her jaw clenches every time a notification pings. Monday evening. Theo Barker's quantitative methods study group. Melanie will offer to help model the LP losses. The approach crystallizes in your dreaming mind with architectural precision—each step, each calculated vulnerability she'll exploit.

Then something the binding didn't intend to show, or maybe it did: Melanie lying awake at 1:30 AM, Rachel unconscious beside her, and the emotion that floods through the dream-link is so layered it takes your sleeping brain a moment to parse. Tenderness. Genuine, uncomplicated tenderness for this broken woman she's methodically rewiring. And underneath it, wound tight as piano wire, a dark electric thrill that borders on erotic—the power of watching someone's entire psychological architecture bend toward you, knowing you built the maze they're lost in.

She loves this. Not performs it, not tolerates it. *Loves* it.

The dream cycles through two more REM periods—fragments now, impressions. Melanie texting Juno Kress about weekend plans, using the bartender's social web to map campus connections. A flash of Rachel's face in morning light, drool on the pillow, and Melanie thinking *mine* with the casual certainty of someone counting inventory. The Priya plan again, refined, angles sharpened.

You surface at 7:15 AM to gray Seattle light leaking around the curtains and a body that feels like it belongs to someone else. The disorientation is exactly what Lilith warned about—thirty seconds of not knowing whose hands these are, whose ceiling that is, whether Rachel Kim is asleep beside you or three thousand miles away.

Sophia's arm is draped across your waist. Lilith is curled on your other side, her sleep shirt rucked up above her hips, the obsidian pentagram pooled in the hollow of her throat. Her lips are slightly parted, and even in sleep her expression carries something satisfied and predatory—whatever she dreamed about Faye, she enjoyed it.

Your nose isn't bleeding. Your head doesn't hurt. You feel rested—genuinely, deeply rested—and you know everything Melanie wanted you to know.

Secret Information
------------------
Lilith's dream about Faye was more vivid and productive than expected. The binding amplified her planted directive into a full tactical rehearsal: she dreamed through three complete sessions with Faye—Tuesday coffee with trust-accelerant tea, Wednesday evening with the sympathy charm embedded in a bookmark she'll gift Faye, and a Thursday session where the pre-binding extension creates a warm resonance Faye will mistake for deepening friendship. The dream also surfaced something Lilith hasn't consciously acknowledged: she's developing genuine romantic interest in Faye that runs parallel to, not in conflict with, the recruitment objective. The binding is using this authentic attraction as fuel for the manipulation—making her more convincing because the warmth isn't entirely performed.

Critical risk: the dream-link's facilitation charm has altered the binding's ambient resonance in the house. The ceramic dish of mugwort-basil ash on the nightstand is still faintly radiating the asynchronous transfer signature. If Faye visits before Wednesday and performs even a casual diagnostic reading, she could detect this secondary architecture layered onto the primary binding—evidence of active, sophisticated network maintenance that contradicts Lilith's 'academic research subject' cover story. The signature will fade naturally over approximately 72 hours.

At Cornell, 7:15 AM Eastern Sunday: Rachel woke at 6:45 AM, found Melanie still asleep, and experienced a moment of lucidity—a flash of recognition that she hasn't been to her own apartment in six days. The thought triggered immediate anxiety per Melanie's installed suggestion. She made herself coffee in Melanie's dorm kitchenette and sat back down on the bed within four minutes. When Melanie wakes, Rachel will mention wanting to 'grab some clothes from home' but will likely be unable to follow through without Melanie accompanying her.

-- Turn 209 --

Action
------
Slip out of bed quietly and make coffee, and then call Melanie to to confirm that what I absorbed was accurate, and to let her marvel at it a bit. Then give her my advice and instructions, starting by getting her to fully acknowledge her attraction to Rachel, and leading her towards  the understanding that she should be turning Rachel into her personal assistant and sex slave. Tell her that she won't truly be able to say she owns Rachel until Rachel is eagerly helping her enslave other women - just the way she became truly owned by me when she started being turned on by the thought of recruiting for me.

Outcome
-------
You ease out from between two sleeping women with the practiced caution of a man disarming a bomb. Sophia murmurs something unintelligible and rolls into the warm depression you left behind. Lilith doesn't stir at all—her face is slack and content, black hair fanned across the pillow like spilled ink, one hand still resting where your chest used to be.

Downstairs, the kitchen is cool and quiet. Gray morning light fills the room through the craftsman windows. You grind beans, fill the French press, and stand barefoot on the tile while steam rises, sorting through the residue of someone else's memories. It's not confusing anymore—more like recalling a movie you watched last night, except the movie was shot in first person and you could feel the protagonist's heartbeat.

You dial Melanie at 7:32 AM Seattle time. 10:32 Eastern. She picks up on the second ring.

"Tell me it worked." Her voice is hushed, conspiratorial. You can hear sheets rustling. Rachel's still there.

"Four-minute induction," you say. "Down from eleven. You were proud of that."

Silence. Then a sharp intake of breath.

"Oh my *god*." She's whispering now, and you can hear her getting out of bed, a door clicking softly shut—she's moved to the hallway. "You saw that? The actual induction?"

"I saw all of it, Mel. Both times she tried to leave. The way her hands shook when she reached for her jacket. That new suggestion you layered in—the one about proximity making her research better. Clean work."

"Holy shit." A breathless little laugh. "Holy *shit*, David. I spent like fifteen minutes doing the review thing before I fell asleep and I wasn't even sure it was—you got the Priya plan too? Monday, Theo's study group?"

"LP loss modeling as the entry point. I saw the whole blueprint."

"This is insane. This is the best thing that's ever—okay, wait, what did I look like from the outside? Was it weird being me?"

"Being five-foot-one with H-cups was an experience. I'll say that much."

She snort-laughs, catches herself, drops back to a whisper. "Rach is still asleep. She tried to get up around seven, made it to the kitchenette, sat right back down. Six days, David. She hasn't been to her own apartment in six days."

"That's what I want to talk about." You pour coffee, black, and lean against the counter. "Rachel. I need you to be honest with me about something."

"Okay."

"You're attracted to her."

The pause is different this time. Not shock—recognition. The sound of someone being caught.

"I..." Melanie exhales. "Yeah. I am. It's not just the power thing, even though that's—I mean, the power thing is *amazing*. But she's... when she falls asleep against me, there's this—" She stops herself. "It's complicated."

"It's not complicated. You're conditioning a beautiful, brilliant woman who trusts you completely and sleeps in your bed every night. Of course you're attracted to her. Stop pretending the tenderness is a side effect."

Another silence. Longer.

"Okay," she says quietly. "Yeah. Okay. I want her."

"Good. Now stop thinking of her as practice and start thinking of her as *yours*. Because that's what she's becoming, Mel. Your personal assistant. Your lover. Your project. She's already restructuring her entire life around you—she needs to eat when you tell her to eat, sleep when you tell her to sleep, and eventually she needs to be getting off on helping you do this to other women."

You can hear Melanie breathing. Fast. Shallow.

"You know how I knew you were really mine?" you continue. "It wasn't when you obeyed me. It wasn't even when you started wanting to obey. It was when you started recruiting. When Sophia's binding turned you on. When you looked at Rachel for the first time and thought *I could do that*. That's when you crossed over."

"Yeah," she whispers. "Yeah, I remember."

"Rachel won't truly be yours until she's eagerly helping you break someone else. Until she's sitting next to Priya in that study group and thinking about how to isolate her for you. *That's* ownership. Everything before that is just training."

The breathing on the other end has gone ragged. When Melanie speaks again, her voice has that thick, slightly stupid quality it gets when arousal starts eroding her higher functions—the hornier-dumber loop the binding installed.

"You're making me wet in a hallway at ten-thirty in the morning."

"Use it. Go back in there. She's going to wake up and ask if she can go grab clothes from her apartment. Tell her you'll go with her. Help her pack a bag. A *big* bag. And when you're there, in her space, surrounded by her things—let her see how much you want her. Not the caretaker. Not the mentor. *You*."

"David..."

"Own her, Mel. All the way. Make her yours, and then make her useful."

She's quiet for three heartbeats. When she speaks, the uncertainty is gone. What's left is the predatory focus you felt in the dream—that piano-wire tension between tenderness and hunger.

"I'll send you the results tonight," she says. "Sweet dreams, boss man."

The line goes dead. You sip your coffee in the gray Seattle morning and listen to the house settle around you.

Melanie returns to her dorm room at 10:38 AM Eastern. Rachel is sitting up in bed, clutching a mug of coffee she made herself, wearing one of Melanie's hoodies. Action
------
Skip ahead to Tuesday evening—debriefing over the phone with Lilith, Sophia, and Melanie about our ongoing projects:
1. Sophia's content numbers as we've introduced more of the faceless dom content, and how initial contact is going with Mila Mondell.
2. Lilith's visit with Faye using the trust enhancing tea and the pre-binding extension

Outcome
-------
Tuesday night. You're on the living room couch with your laptop open to Sophia's analytics dashboard, a half-eaten bowl of pad see ew balanced on the armrest, and your phone on speaker between two throw pillows. Lilith sits cross-legged on the floor by the coffee table, still in her coat—she got back from Faye's apartment twenty minutes ago and hasn't stopped moving since, pulling herb pouches and her Moleskine out of her bag like a field medic unpacking after triage. Sophia is curled in the armchair with her knees drawn up, scrolling her own phone, red hair piled in a messy bun.

Melanie's voice fills the room, tinny through the speaker but bright with energy. It's almost eleven her time.

"Okay, who goes first? I have *news*."

"Soph," you say. "Numbers."

Sophia taps her screen and reads without looking up. "Week two closed at sixty-one-eight. Sixty-one thousand, eight hundred dollars. The faceless dom teaser pulled twenty-two thousand DMs in forty-eight hours—I had to hire a chatting service to handle overflow, which cost me four hundred bucks and was worth every cent. PPV unlock rate on the extended cut was eleven percent, which is obscene. Industry average is three."

"Jesus," Melanie says.

"The algorithm loves the mystery angle. Who's the guy, what does he look like, are they really together. I'm getting fan edits on TikTok. Someone made a thirst trap compilation of just my *reactions* during the preview clip and it has six hundred thousand views." Sophia pauses. "Also, Mila Mondell replied to my DM."

The room goes quiet.

"She said—and I'm quoting—'honestly I've been watching your comeback and it's making me feel things about my own hiatus lol. would love to talk if you're open to it.' I sent back something warm but not desperate. We're texting. She's fragile right now, you can feel it in every message. Lots of ellipses. Lots of 'idk if this makes sense but.' She hasn't posted content in nineteen days."

"Don't rush her," you say.

"I'm not. I'm being exactly what she needs—someone who gets it, who came back stronger, who isn't going to judge her for whatever sent her offline." Sophia's voice softens. "She's lonely, David. Like I was."

You let that sit for a beat, then turn to Lilith. "How was Faye?"

Lilith pulls the cap off a pen with her teeth and spits it onto the carpet. "Good. Really good. I brewed the basil-anise blend into a chai base so it didn't taste like I was drugging her, which—I mean, I was, but subtlety matters." She flips open the Moleskine. "We spent three hours on her grandmother's veve reconstruction. She's got maybe sixty percent of the routing framework decoded now. The missing forty percent is the part that would let us channel binding communication through a lwa intermediary instead of brute-forcing it through our own nervous systems."

"And the trust tea?"

Lilith's black lips curve. "She drank two cups. By the second one she was showing me pages from her grandmother's notebook that she said she'd never shown anyone. Original ink diagrams from the nineteen-fifties. Her hands were shaking when she turned the pages—not from fear, from *excitement*. She's been sitting on this knowledge alone for years and she's starving for someone who takes it seriously."

"Did you give her the bookmark?"

Lilith nods. "Slipped it between the pages of a binding theory text I lent her. The sympathy charm is woven into the thread. She'll be handling it every time she studies, which knowing Faye is about four hours a day. By Thursday the resonance should feel like background noise—familiar, warm, something she associates with our sessions without knowing why."

"She suspect anything?"

"She's too happy to suspect. That's the thing about Faye—she's brilliant and cautious, but she's also *lonely*. When I laugh at her jokes and ask the right questions about her grandmother's techniques, she lights up like a kid at Christmas. I'm giving her something she's never had. A peer." Lilith pauses, and something complicated crosses her face—a flicker of guilt, maybe, or its cousin. "She hugged me when I left. She's not a hugger."

Melanie clears her throat on the speaker. "My turn?"

"Go."

"So. Rachel." A pause loaded with something humid and self-satisfied. "We slept together Sunday. Like, *slept together* slept together. At her apartment, while she was packing a bag to bring back to my room. I kissed her and she just—collapsed into it. Like she'd been holding her breath for a week and I was oxygen."

Sophia raises an eyebrow at you from the armchair.

"She's sleeping in my bed every night with a full bag of her things in my closet. She cooks for me now. Monday morning she reorganized my desk without being asked and had my pharmacology notes color-coded before I woke up. When I came out of the shower she was sitting on the bed holding my coffee like a—" Melanie laughs, that genuine dorky snort. "Like a wife in a fifties commercial. It's adorable. And *hot*. Both things at once."

"And you're enjoying her," you say. Not a question.

"David." Her voice drops, goes thick. "Last night I made her kneel on the floor while I studied. Just—kneel there, next to my chair, with her head on my thigh. For two hours. She didn't complain. She didn't fidget. When I finally looked down at her she had this *expression*—like she'd found the exact place in the world she was supposed to be. And I came so hard that night I almost bit through my pillow."

Lilith's pen has stopped moving.

"Priya," you prompt.

"Right. Monday evening, Theo's study group. Eight people around a table in Olin Library. Priya showed up twenty minutes late looking like she'd slept in her car—which, honestly, she might have. I'd positioned myself next to Theo so when she sat down, the only open seat was across from me. I waited forty minutes before I said a single word to her. Let her stew in her own stress. Then when the group broke for coffee I said, very casually, 'You look like someone who's running numbers that won't cooperate.'"

Sophia snorts.

"She looked at me like I'd slapped her. Then she said, 'Is it that obvious?' And I said, 'Only to someone who's been there.' We talked for twelve minutes. I didn't push. I asked about her fund structure—general stuff, nothing invasive—and offered to look at her LP attrition model. She said she'd think about it. Then this morning she texted me. Wants to meet Thursday." Melanie's satisfaction is almost tangible through the phone speaker. "I'm in the door."

You lean back into the couch cushions, the pad see ew forgotten. Three operations running on three separate tracks, each one advancing steadily, and the dream-link feeding you nightly updates so detailed you can practically taste Melanie's coffee.

"Good girls," you say. "All of you."

Lilith looks up from her Moleskine. Sophia smiles from behind her phone. On the speaker, Melanie exhales like she's been waiting to hear exactly those words.

Secret Information
------------------
The mugwort-basil ash residue from Saturday's dream-link facilitation charm has faded as of Tuesday morning—the 72-hour window has passed. Familiar. She won't associate it with me specifically—it'll just feel like her apartment is cozier when she's studying binding theory."

Lilith nods. "Exactly. Without the pre-binding extension, Faye walks into a house saturated with desire-based binding architecture and her first instinct is to diagnose it. But it means the charm is leaving a footprint I didn't account for. She scribbles a note, pen moving fast. "I can fold chamomile and white sage ash into the base. It'll muddy any fine-grained diagnostic reading she tries to run for about forty-eight hours after ingestion. That covers Thursday evening through Saturday, which is when I want her here."

"I planted the seed and let the desire-extension water it. By Thursday she was asking me questions about you unprompted—what you look like, how we met, whether you practice."

Melanie's voice comes through the laptop: "What about me?"

"You're my sister who goes to Cornell. Pre-med, brilliant, beautiful. I told Faye that you're part of our household even from a distance—that we share something deeper than blood. I described our dynamic as chosen family with... flexible boundaries." Lilith pauses. "Her eyes got wide when I said 'flexible.' She didn't ask me to clarify. She just said, 'That sounds liberating.'"

Sophia looks up from the floor. "And me?"

"You're the one I was most careful with. Faye knows a woman named Sophia lives here—a content creator who came to us after a stalking situation. I framed you as someone who found safety in our household and chose to stay because of what we offer. I told her you're stunning, fiercely independent, and that watching you come back to life after what happened to you was one of the most beautiful things I'd ever seen." Lilith glances at Sophia. "I may have also mentioned that you and I have become very close."

"Define 'very close,'" Sophia says.

"I let her infer. Faye's not stupid—she pieced together that this household doesn't operate on conventional relationship rules. And instead of being put off, she was *fascinated*. She asked me Wednesday, 'Is everyone in your house in love with each other?' and I said, 'Not exactly. But everyone in my house belongs to each other in some way.' And she got this look—hungry and scared and curious all at once—and whispered, 'I've never had that.'"

The room is quiet for a beat.

"What about the binding?" you ask. "Your binding. Does she suspect?"

"She sensed a network around me at our first coffee. Her word—*network*. I deflected with ward signatures and amulet resonance. The tea's been dampening her investigative instinct since, but she *knows* something about me doesn't quite scan." Lilith exhales. "The genius of the polyamory framing is that it explains the network she's sensing without her needing to dig deeper. Multiple intimate bonds between magical practitioners *would* create detectable resonance patterns. She's interpreting the binding as love, basically. Which... isn't entirely wrong."

"The grandmother's notebooks?" you press.

"Outer notebooks only—theory, historical context, basic veves. But Friday she told me she wants to show me the inner ones. The actual lwa-routing technique. Before the extension she'd have guarded those until she trusted me for a year. Now she's ready to hand them over because she wants me to see all of her."

Melanie leans into her camera. "So when she walks in tomorrow and finds all four of us, it's not a surprise—it's the reveal she's been hoping for."

Secret Information
------------------
Lilith's account is accurate but strategically curated even under the spell's honesty compulsion—she told the full truth but presented it in the most favorable light. What she omitted: Faye's diagnostic at the first coffee meeting detected not just a 'network' but specifically a hierarchical structure with David at the apex. The polyamory framing successfully recontextualized this as an intimate power dynamic rather than magical coercion, but Faye's notes from that meeting (which Lilith hasn't seen) include the phrase 'one source, multiple channels—intentional?' If Faye reviews those notes before Saturday's ritual, she might reconsider her interpretation. The desire-extension is currently strong enough to override this risk, but the window matters.

Faye's Wednesday question ('Is everyone in your house in love with each other?') was prompted by a dream she had Tuesday night in which she saw four women arranged around a man in a candlelit room. She attributed this to her Erzulie Freda connection showing her Lilith's household dynamic. In reality, the dream was generated by ambient residue from the dream-link facilitation charm that hadn't fully faded from the Craftsman's master bedroom. Faye essentially received a fragmentary, distorted echo of a dream-link session. This is both fortunate (it primed her curiosity about the household) and dangerous (it means her Erzulie channel is sensitive enough to pick up ambient magical signatures in the house).

Secret Information
------------------

I'd already felt what the binding felt like secondhand through Lilith, even if I didn't realize what it was at the time. Lilith chews her lip. On screen, Melanie is watching silently, chin resting on her fist.

"She won't know it's a binding," Lilith says carefully. "Not in those terms. Not at first."

"Explain."

"The circle I'm drawing isn't a standard binding array. It's a collaborative veve—or it looks like one. I've designed it to mirror the lwa-routing structure from her grandmother's notebooks. "Yes," Lilith says. No flinch. No apology. Just the fact of it, laid bare.

Secret Information
------------------
Lilith's plan to disguise the binding as a lwa-routing activation is genuine and well-constructed, but carries significant risk she hasn't fully articulated. Additionally, if Erzulie Freda responds to the invocation and perceives the binding architecture hidden within the lwa-routing veve, the lwa's reaction is completely unpredictable. Lilith is gambling that Erzulie—a spirit of love, desire, and luxury—will view the binding as consistent with her domain rather than as a violation of her devotee.

Sophia's question to David ('Can you live with that?') reflects genuine curiosity rather than moral challenge. Her own binding's adjustment mechanism has fully integrated; she views her consent situation with detached acceptance and finds others' moral wrestling mildly fascinating. She asked because she wants to understand David's psychology, not because she's troubled.

Melanie stayed silent during the reveal because she's already processed the ethics and moved past them. Her primary concern is logistical: whether the disguised binding is mechanically sound enough to work on a practitioner of Faye's caliber.

"Are you happier this way?" I ask her. When she replies in the affirmative, as I know she will, then I say. "Then I can live with it. But, I do want a backup plan. What happens if Erzulie doesn't play along, or Faye's diagnostics catch the binding mid-ritual? What's the play then?"

Outcome
-------
You look at Sophia with a small smile. "Are you happier this way?"

She doesn't hesitate. Doesn't perform. She just meets your eyes with that steady jade-green gaze and says, "I made sixty-one thousand dollars last week doing something I'm good at, in a house where nobody's going to hurt me, surrounded by people who actually give a shit whether I'm okay. My stalker is selling candles on Shopify. I sleep eight hours a night." She tucks the pencil behind her ear. "Yeah, David. I'm happier this way."

"Then I can live with it."

Lilith exhales—not quite relief, something closer to a knot loosening between her shoulder blades. On screen, Melanie's expression doesn't change, but you catch the micro-nod.

"But," you continue, "I want a backup plan. What happens if Erzulie doesn't play along, or Faye's diagnostics catch the binding mid-ritual? What's the play then?"

Lilith pulls at a thread on the couch cushion. She's quiet for longer than you'd expect.

"If Erzulie actively resists," she says slowly, "we'll know immediately. The room temperature drops. The candles gutter. Faye will feel it through her body like a door slamming. At that point the veve collapses and the binding architecture goes with it. No harm done to Faye—she just feels a failed ritual, which happens. I frame it as a resonance mismatch, apologize, suggest we try again after recalibrating. We lose the Saturday window but we don't lose Faye."

"And if her diagnostics catch it?"

That pause is longer.

"That's the bad scenario," Lilith admits. "If Faye senses the binding architecture *while it's actively forming*—before it completes—she'll know exactly what it is. She's not some dabbler who read a blog. She grew up watching her grandmother route spirits through hand-drawn channels. She'll recognize coercion."

Sophia shifts on the floor. "So she bolts."

"She bolts, and she's furious, and she has the diagnostic vocabulary to describe what we tried to do to her. She won't go to the cops—this isn't a cops thing—but she could ward herself so thoroughly that we'd never get within fifty feet of her again. And the grandmother's notebooks go with her."

Melanie's voice, clinical: "Can we contain it in the room?"

"Not magically. Not against a practitioner mid-diagnostic. But..." Lilith looks at you. "Sophia's binding is desire-dominant. If I ramp the ambient resonance in the room high enough—all four of us projecting—Faye's Erzulie connection will be flooded with competing signals. It's not a block, it's noise. Like trying to hear a whisper at a concert. It might buy enough time for the binding to finish anchoring."

"Might," you repeat.

"Seventy-thirty in our favor. Maybe seventy-five. The extension is doing heavy lifting—her desire for me, for this household, for what we represent—that's not fake. The magic amplified it, but the foundation is real. Even if she catches a glimpse of the architecture, part of her is going to *want* to ignore it."

Sophia stretches her arms overhead. "What about after? If she catches it after the binding completes?"

"Then the adjustment mechanism handles it. Same as you. Initial distress, rapid smoothing, acceptance within seventy-two hours. She'll be angry, then confused, then... not." Lilith picks up her wine glass again. "The binding doesn't care whether you consented. It only cares that you're in it."

The rain picks up against the windows. Somewhere upstairs, a pipe groans.

Secret Information
------------------
Lilith's seventy-thirty estimate is optimistic. Her actual confidence level is closer to sixty-forty if Faye's diagnostics activate mid-ritual. The desire-frequency resonance with Erzulie Freda cuts both ways: it floods Faye with desire but also keeps her spiritual senses at peak sensitivity. The 'noise' strategy of ramping ambient resonance from all four bound women could work, but it requires precise emotional synchronization that they haven't rehearsed. If even one participant's projection wavers—if Melanie's jet lag breaks her focus, or Sophia's nervousness spikes—the noise floor drops and Faye's diagnostic clarity returns.

Sophia's answer to David's question was entirely genuine. The binding's adjustment mechanism completed its work weeks ago; she experiences her current life as an authentic improvement. Her observation about David's question was internal: she noted that he asked *her* rather than simply deciding, and filed it as evidence that he's still capable of moral consideration despite everything.

Action

I turn to Lilith. "I'm sure you've considered this backwards and forwards, but it's worth asking - is there a way to get Faye to willingly consent to the binding—even partially—rather than hiding it entirely? A middle path where she knows something is being offered, even if not the full scope. Or will she be too likely to pick up on the true intent if she's told there's a binding in the first place?"

Outcome
-------
Lilith tilts her head, and you watch something shift behind those electric blue contacts—not surprise, exactly, but the recognition that you've asked the one question she's been circling for days without landing on.

"I've thought about it," she says. "Believe me, I've thought about it." She sets the wine glass on the side table and draws her knees up, wrapping her arms around them. The obsidian pentagram swings forward, catching lamplight. "There are... technically three versions of how this could go."

She holds up one finger. "Version one is what I just described. Full concealment. She thinks she's participating in a lwa-routing activation. Binding piggybacks underneath. Highest success probability, lowest consent."

Second finger. "Version two is full transparency. 'Hey Faye, we have a magical household where everyone is bound to one man, want to join?' She runs. Immediately. Not because the concept horrifies her—honestly, her Erzulie practice has room for devotional surrender—but because she'd recognize the coercive architecture. She'd know we were offering a leash, not a partnership."

Third finger. "Version three. The middle path you're describing. I tell her something real but incomplete. Something like: 'We share a sacred bond. It's deeper than love—it's magical infrastructure. Erzulie can carry you into it if you're willing. You'll feel connected to all of us in a way that changes you permanently.' That's all true. Every word."

"But it leaves out the obedience component," Sophia says from the floor.

"It leaves out the obedience component," Lilith confirms. "And the irrevocability. And the fact that David sits at the center of it like a spider."

Melanie speaks up from the laptop: "Would version three actually change anything mechanically? Same ritual, same binding, she just has a slightly more accurate map going in?"

"That's the thing." Lilith bites the corner of her lower lip. "It might actually *improve* the binding. Consent—even partial, even uninformed—creates a sympathetic channel that pure deception doesn't. Her grandmother's notebooks describe something called *ouvèti volontè*. Voluntary opening. When a devotee willingly steps into a lwa's embrace, the connection is stronger, cleaner, more durable than one imposed by force. If Faye *chooses* to enter the circle knowing that something permanent and transformative is being offered, even without knowing the full scope, the binding could anchor deeper than Sophia's did."

Sophia raises an eyebrow but doesn't look offended.

"The risk," Lilith continues, leaning forward, "is that giving her any information activates her diagnostic instincts. Right now the extension is keeping those instincts foggy and pleasure-drunk. If I say the word 'bond' or 'binding' to her face, even framed as sacred, some part of her brain lights up and starts scanning. And if she scans during the ritual instead of surrendering to it..."

"We're back to the seventy-thirty scenario," you say.

"Maybe sixty-forty with version three, because she'd be actively looking. But if she *doesn't* scan—if Erzulie and the extension and her own desire carry her past that threshold—then the binding we get is significantly more robust."

Lilith looks at you directly. "Higher risk. Higher reward. Your call, David."

Secret Information
------------------
Lilith's description of ouvèti volontè is accurate—the concept exists in Faye's grandmother's outer notebooks and describes a principle where voluntary participation in spiritual bonding creates stronger, more stable connections. What Lilith hasn't fully worked through is that the ouvèti volontè principle has a corollary: if a devotee discovers post-facto that the bond was significantly different from what they consented to, the betrayal of trust can cause the bond to destabilize in ways that pure coercion bonds don't. Essentially, version three creates a binding that's stronger if it holds but more fragile if challenged. This is a theoretical concern—the adjustment mechanism should prevent Faye from challenging it—but it represents a genuine structural difference from Sophia's binding.

Sophia's lack of offense at the suggestion her binding might be weaker is genuine. She doesn't experience her binding as something that could be improved or degraded—it simply is. Her internal reaction to version three is practical curiosity about whether a stronger Faye binding would benefit the household's magical infrastructure.

It hurts for a bit and then it doesn't."

She pauses, crossing her arms over her chest.

"But Faye isn't me. I was running from a stalker. I was desperate. My defenses were already shredded. Faye is a practitioner who grew up inside this stuff. If the adjustment mechanism has to fight against someone who *understands* what's been done to her on a structural level—someone who can name the specific architecture of what's holding her—does it still work the same way? I genuinely don't know. Lilith?"

Lilith opens her mouth, then closes it. "I... think so. The mechanism doesn't care about intellectual understanding. It works on emotional architecture."

"You *think* so," Sophia repeats flatly.

From the laptop, Melanie's voice cuts through with that particular clarity she gets when she's been thinking three steps ahead. "I have a different angle. Forget the binding mechanics for a second. Think about what we actually *want* from Faye long-term."

She shifts on her bed, and you catch a glimpse of Rachel's dark hair on the pillow behind her, chest rising and falling in deep sleep.

"If we want Faye's notebooks and her lwa-routing technique and her cooperation building distance infrastructure—version three is better. Not just because the binding's stronger. Because she'll *identify* with the household. She'll think she chose this. That's worth more than a clean deception that she might eventually reconstruct and resent."

"Even if the resentment gets smoothed over by the adjustment mechanism?" you ask.

"Smoothed over isn't the same as gone," Melanie says. "Rachel doesn't resent me because she genuinely chose to trust me before I ever revealed anything. That foundation matters. The mechanism is a safety net, not a substitute for actual buy-in."

Sophia nods slowly. "She's right. And there's something else. If we're going to be doing rituals with Faye—complex ones, ones that require her grandmother's techniques—we need her engaged, not just compliant. There's a difference between a bound person who follows orders and a bound person who's *invested*."

Lilith has gone very still, watching this exchange like someone seeing furniture rearranged in her own living room. You recognize the expression—it's the look she gets when a conclusion she'd been avoiding gets articulated by someone else.

"The risk is real, though," Lilith says quietly. "If I frame it as a sacred bond and she scans mid-ritual, the partial honesty actually makes the betrayal worse. She'll feel like I lured her in with just enough truth to make the lie stick."

"Then don't let it be a lie," Melanie says. "Tell her something true enough that even if she scans, what she finds matches what you promised. Sacred bond. Permanent transformation. Connection to all of us. The rain has thickened outside. Sophia looks at you. Lilith looks at you. Melanie's face on the screen, half-lit by her desk lamp, looks at you.

Three women waiting for a verdict.

Secret Information

"Twelve minutes ago she texted. On the light rail," Lilith says, scrolling her phone. "One-thirty arrival."

April drizzle beads on the windshield. You don't bother with wipers.

"How's the extrapolation holding up?"

"Solid. Went through it three times this morning. The lwa-routing channels are the first thing she'll notice—that's the bait. The binding geometry is threaded through the decorative filigree underneath. She'd need to sit with it for twenty uninterrupted minutes, fully diagnostic, to isolate the secondary layer." "My contribution works."

"I know." No sarcasm. Just certainty.

You swing onto Broadway. Three blocks out. The glass canopy of Capitol Hill station shimmers with rain.

"There," Lilith murmurs.

Faye Desrosiers stands ten feet from the escalator exit, apart from the umbrella-clutching commuters. She's shorter than you expected—five-four, maybe five-five—with soft, angular features and warm brown skin a shade lighter than milk chocolate. Her hair is a cascade of tight dark curls spilling past one shoulder; the other side is shaved clean to the skin in a sharp asymmetric cut that gives her the look of someone who walked out of a Bushwick gallery opening. Purple lipstick, vivid against her complexion. She wears an oversized moss-green corduroy jacket over a cropped white tee and high-waisted black jeans, a heavy canvas messenger bag riding her hip. No umbrella. The mist settles on her bare shoulder and she doesn't flinch.

She's scanning the street with dark, intelligent eyes—searching without urgency. Beautiful in a way that sneaks up on you: the elegant line of her jaw, the fullness of her mouth.

Lilith leans between the seats. "Front seat. You're the unknown quantity—the partner she's been curious about since I described the household. Let her size you up. I'm the anchor she already trusts."

You ease toward the curb. Faye's gaze finds the Subaru, then finds Lilith through the rear window. Something shifts in her expression—a softening, a pull—before her eyes travel forward to you behind the wheel.

Curiosity. Appraisal. A flicker of something hotter underneath.

"That's David?" Faye asks, quieter now.

"That's David."

"He's... not what I pictured."

"What did you picture?"

Up close, her features are striking. High cheekbones that catch shadows. Dark brown eyes with an unusual amber ring around the iris—natural, unlike Lilith's theatrical contacts. The shaved side of her head reveals a small tattoo behind her ear: a veve you don't recognize, done in fine black ink.

"David." She extends her hand. Her grip is firm, her palm warm and dry despite the rain. "Lilith talks about you like you're some kind of gravitational anomaly. I figured I should come see what all the mass was about."

"Faye." You hold her hand exactly one beat longer than polite. "She talks about you the same way."

Something flickers behind those amber-ringed eyes. She withdraws her hand slowly, and you notice her fingertips brush your palm on the way out—deliberate or unconscious, hard to say.

From the back seat, Lilith's voice: "The house is about twelve minutes from here. Sophia and Melanie are already setting up."

Faye buckles her seatbelt, glances at you one more time, then faces forward. "Drive, gravitational anomaly. Show me what you've built."

Faye's posture shifts—subtle, but you catch it in your peripheral vision. Her hand goes to the messenger bag on her lap, protective. "She told you about those?"

"She tells me everything that matters to her. And you matter to her, so." You glance over, brief, warm. "By extension, I've been looking forward to meeting you for about two weeks."

Silence. Then Faye exhales something that might be a laugh. "Two weeks. She's been talking about me for two weeks?"

"Longer," Lilith says from the back. "But I started using the word 'brilliant' about two weeks ago. Before that it was just 'interesting.' David knows the difference."

"There's a grading scale," you say.

"There's absolutely a grading scale," Lilith confirms.

Faye turns in her seat to look at Lilith, and you see something unguarded pass between them—Faye searching, Lilith holding steady, letting herself be found. When Faye turns back, the tension in her shoulders has dropped another notch.

"So what's the household like?" she asks. "Lilith described it as... collaborative."

"It's four people who are genuinely good at different things, figuring out what happens when you stop pretending those things don't overlap." You brake for a red light at Fifteenth and Madison. "Sophia's a choreographer—she thinks in bodies and space. Melanie's a strategist. Lilith does the deep work. I mostly drive."

Faye snorts. "You mostly drive."

"And occasionally say something useful."

From the back: "He's being modest. He's the reason all of it holds together. He just doesn't need you to know that yet."

You meet Lilith's eyes in the rearview. She winks—slow, deliberate, performative enough for Faye to catch in her peripheral vision. The gesture says: *we do this. We play. It's warm in here.*

Faye registers it. You watch her process—the easy shorthand between you and Lilith, the absence of jealousy or ownership in Lilith's tone, the way Lilith's compliment landed without you needing to claim it. Her fingers relax on the messenger bag strap.

"You know I'm sizing you up," Faye says quietly.

"I'd be disappointed if you weren't."

"And you're not nervous about that."

You turn onto Fifteenth Avenue. Three blocks from the Craftsman. Through the rain-streaked windshield, you can see the porch light Sophia left on.

"It's Fenty. Violet Fury," she says. "Discontinued two years ago. I have six tubes stockpiled in my bathroom like a doomsday prepper."

"Monotone is a statement," you agree. "The statement is 'I own one lipstick.'"

"Smooth."

"Sincere, actually. The smooth part is accidental."
